Heredoc strings support variable interpolation (like double-quoted strings), while nowdoc strings (delimited with single quotes) treat variables literally, like single-quoted strings.
The sort() function reindexes array keys numerically; use asort() to sort while preserving key associations.
In PHP, string keys that are valid integer representations (like '5') are automatically cast to integers when used as array keys.
in_array() uses loose comparison (==) by default; the third parameter $strict must be set to true to use strict comparison (===).
Without a callback, array_filter() removes all elements that evaluate to false (falsy values: false, 0, '', '0', null, []).
The $preserve_keys parameter of array_slice() defaults to false, so keys are reindexed by default.

Constructor property promotion was introduced in PHP 8.0, allowing visibility modifiers to be added to constructor parameters to automatically declare and assign them as properties.
The 'final' keyword in PHP prevents a method from being overridden in subclasses.
In PHP, the final keyword on a method prevents any subclass from overriding it.
Private properties are only accessible within the class where they are defined, not in subclasses.
In PHP, private methods are hidden from child classes, so a child can freely declare a method with the same name and any visibility without conflict.
__get() is called for both inaccessible (protected/private) properties and non-existent properties, not only for non-existent ones.
Reassigning an already-initialized readonly property in PHP throws an \Error, not an \Exception.
PHP interfaces can declare public constants, which are accessible and cannot be overridden by implementing classes.

Since PHP 8.0, interfaces can declare static methods, which implementing classes must also provide as static methods.
The instanceof operator in PHP checks both class inheritance and interface implementation, so an object that implements an interface will return true for instanceof against that interface.
Interface methods in PHP can only declare a signature without any implementation; they cannot have a method body like trait methods can.
In PHP, abstract methods can be declared as public or protected (and since PHP 7.1, even private), so protected visibility is allowed.

In PHP, both Exception and Error implement the Throwable interface, making it their common ancestor in the type hierarchy.

The @ operator suppresses errors (warnings, notices) but does not suppress exceptions; exceptions still propagate up the call stack.

Functions registered with register_shutdown_function() are executed during the shutdown sequence, which occurs after exit or die halts normal script execution.

In PHP, variables defined in the global scope are not accessible inside a function unless explicitly imported via 'global', accessed through '$GLOBALS', or passed as parameters.

yield from (PHP 7.0+) delegates iteration to another generator or Traversable, forwarding its values to the caller.

SplStack implements a LIFO (Last In, First Out) stack, not a FIFO queue; SplQueue is the one that implements FIFO.

password_hash() internally generates a random salt and embeds it in the resulting hash string; there is no parameter to supply one separately.

PHP traits can declare constants, which are then accessible in the class that uses the trait.
In PHP, casting any object to bool always returns true.
The array_find() function has not been introduced in any PHP version as of the latest releases; it remains a long-standing community proposal but is not part of PHP's built-in functions.
Property hooks (get/set defined directly in the property declaration) were indeed introduced in PHP 8.4.
Asymmetric visibility (e.g., public private(set) string $name) was indeed introduced as a new feature in PHP 8.4.
The #[NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.4 to mark return types whose values should not be silently discarded.
The pipe operator |> was introduced in PHP 8.4, allowing chained function calls in a pipeline style.
